FALSIFIABLE
Open, but could be disproved with a finite counterexample.
Let $G$ be a graph with chromatic number $k$ containing no $K_k$. If $a,b\geq 2$ and $a+b=k+1$ then must there exist two disjoint subgraphs of $G$ with chromatic numbers $\geq a$ and $\geq b$ respectively?
#628: [Er68b]
graph theory | 
chromatic number
This property is sometimes called being $(a,b)$-splittable. A question of Erdős and Lovász (often called the Erdős-Lovász Tihany conjecture). Erdős [Er68b] originally asked about $a=b=3$ which was proved by Brown and Jung [BrJu69] (who in fact prove that $G$ must contain two vertex disjoint odd cycles).
Balogh, Kostochka, Prince, and Stiebitz [BKPS09] have proved the full conjecture for quasi-line graphs and graphs with independence number $2$.
For more partial results in this direction see the comprehensive survey of this problem by Song [So22].
See also the entry in the graphs problem collection.
Additional thanks to: Quanyu Tang

 The order-13 double-critical census, completed at $k = 6$ and $k = 7$.
Prior work. The $a = 2$ case of Erdős–Lovász Tihany ($b = k-1$) reduces to the Double-Critical Graph Conjecture: every connected double-critical $k$-chromatic graph is $K_k$, where double-critical means $\chi(G-\{x,y\}) = k-2$ for every edge $xy$. Connectedness is not decoration: $K_k$ plus an isolated vertex is $k$-chromatic and double-critical and is not $K_k$. None of that reduction is ours, and neither is the $\le 12$ result it is checked against.
$k \le 5$, at every order, is Stiebitz, "Subgraphs of colour-critical graphs", Combinatorica 7 (1987) 303–312.
"No noncomplete connected double-critical graph on at most 12 vertices" is usually cited to Kriesell and Pedersen (Discrete Math. Theor. Comput. Sci. 17:2 (2015)), where it is asserted in the introduction, p. 50. The proof is elsewhere: an unpublished two-page note, A. S. Pedersen, "No non-complete double-critical graph on less than 13 vertices", 24 September 2012. Its host URL is dead; the copy we read is at web.archive.org/web/20170829001215/http://imada.sdu.dk/~asp/noSmallNonCompleteDC.pdf. That note is not a census, and the present computation is not a bigger version of it. It combines Stiebitz's $k \le 5$; the Kawarabayashi–Pedersen–Toft bound that a 6-chromatic example needs at least 12 vertices; one SAGE check against Royle's catalogue of 12-vertex 6-chromatic edge-critical graphs; and Gallai's decomposability theorem, whose hypothesis $n \le 2\chi-2$ holds at $n = 12$ for every $\chi \ge 7$, with equality in the boundary case $\chi = 7$. That boundary is that argument's stop, not an artefact of computing power: at $n = 13$ the hypothesis needs $\chi \ge 8$, so the 7-chromatic case falls outside it and the argument does not reach it. (Two details for anyone following the citation trail. The DMTCS introduction describes the $\le 12$ result as obtained with SAGE and nauty geng; the note itself uses SAGE against Royle's catalogue and no geng. And since the note is not a census, our own $\le 12$ numbers below are checked against the report's census and against the note's statement — no published table of counts at $\le 12$ exists to match them against.)
Order 13 was opened by a working report at erdosproblemaday.com/report/628 (AI-disclosed, marked PARTIAL, 27 July 2026), which also ran its own $\le 12$ census. It carried order 13 to $k = 8, 9, 10, 11$, stopped there, and left $(k,n) = (6,13)$ and $(7,13)$ open with an estimate of about $1.06 \times 10^{10}$ candidates for the former. The framing below is the report's, unchanged: its Lemma 2 (a $K_k$-free $k$-chromatic non-$(2,k-1)$-splittable graph contains an induced noncomplete double-critical $k$-chromatic subgraph) and its Corollary 4, which is Proposition 9 of Kawarabayashi, Pedersen and Toft (arXiv:0810.3133 (= Electron. J. Combin. 17(1) (2010), DOI 10.37236/359)): a connected noncomplete double-critical $k$-chromatic graph with $k \ge 6$ has $\delta \ge k+1$, hence at least $k+2$ vertices. The candidate space, the generation command and the filter order are all theirs.
What is claimed. There is no noncomplete connected double-critical $k$-chromatic graph on 13 vertices, for $k = 6$ and for $k = 7$. Those were the two open cells. Five counts per cell, each computed twice:
$(k,n) = (7,13)$: generated 77,423,446; $K_k$-free 68,389,280; $\chi = k$ 5,332,525; $(2,k-1)$-splittable 5,332,525; survivors 0
$(k,n) = (6,13)$: generated 12,371,706,156; $K_k$-free 8,036,464,642; $\chi = k$ 2,468,617,015; $(2,k-1)$-splittable 2,468,617,015; survivors 0
"Generated" is the connected graphs on 13 vertices with $\delta \ge k+1$; a survivor would be a noncomplete double-critical $k$-chromatic graph, i.e. a counterexample candidate. Every one of the 2,468,617,015 graphs with $\chi = 6$ had an edge $xy$ with $\chi(G-\{x,y\}) \ge 5$, and the split witness was verified on each. In all four runs the $\chi = k$ column equals splittable plus survivors. The word "connected" is in the claim because geng was run with -c; given Proposition 9 it costs nothing at this order, since a disconnected graph with $\delta \ge k+1$ needs $2(k+2) \ge 16$ vertices.
The $K_k$-free filter costs nothing either, for an elementary reason. Suppose a connected double-critical $k$-chromatic graph contains a $K_k$ and has a vertex outside it. Connectedness then gives an edge $uv$ with $v$ in the clique and $u$ outside it — take the first edge of a shortest path leaving the clique. Deleting $u$ and $v$ leaves the other $k-1$ clique vertices, so $\chi(G-\{u,v\}) \ge k-1$, while double-criticality demands $k-2$. Hence a connected double-critical $k$-chromatic graph containing $K_k$ is $K_k$ itself, and every noncomplete connected candidate is $K_k$-free automatically. The filter saves time; it does not narrow what the claim covers.
The measured $(6,13)$ candidate count is 17% above the report's single-shard extrapolation, which warned that "shard balance is not guaranteed."
Order 13 therefore closes, from four sources, one of them ours. $k \le 5$ is known for all orders and is not ours. $k = 6, 7$ is the work above. $k = 8, \ldots, 11$ is the report's, reproduced here as a control before any new cell was run. $k \ge 12$ is vacuous at $n = 13$ by $n \ge k+2$. Within our increment, $(7,13)$ was nearly within the report's own reach — 77 million graphs, 291 core-seconds; it stopped at 199 s without a total. The substantial new computation is $(6,13)$, 12.4 billion graphs.
How it was checked.
Controls first, before either new cell. The whole $\le 12$ census reproduced against the report, cell for cell, the largest class included: $(6,12)$ gives 7,808,882 generated, 4,569,560 $K_6$-free, 1,379,838 with $\chi = 6$. All four of the report's closed order-13 cells reproduced exactly. Ten planted graphs decided correctly: $K_3 \ldots K_7$ accepted as double-critical, and $C_5$, $C_7$, $W_5$, $K_{3,3}$ and the Grötzsch graph rejected with the failing edge printed. Flipping the sense of the double-criticality test breaks all ten.
Paired algorithms. Every predicate that can change a count — clique, chromatic number — is decided twice inside the scanner by algorithms sharing no code path (lowest-vertex-first clique recursion against an include/exclude search for an independent $k$-set in the complement; DSATUR branch-and-bound against a recursive cover by independent sets). A disagreement aborts the worker rather than being averaged into a total. Across roughly $2.5 \times 10^{10}$ scans there were none. Mutation tests confirm the abort path fails closed, and the harvester refuses to print a total unless every shard is present exactly once.
Run twice, differently. Each new cell was computed on x86_64 and on arm64, with separately built geng and scanner binaries and with different shard decompositions: $(6,13)$ at mod 1000 and mod 997, $(7,13)$ at mod 100 and mod 97, the primes chosen so the candidate space is cut differently and the shard-coverage logic is actually tested. All five counts identical in both cells.
A cross-version reproduction, at hash level. A nauty 2.9.3 build — a different release, and a different platform, from the two source-built 2.8.8 production passes — reproduced all 100 $(7,13)$ shards and all 1000 $(6,13)$ shards byte-identically, FNV-1a stream hashes included.
An oracle sharing no idea with the scanner. Both paired colouring algorithms are search procedures over canonically ordered vertices; that is the one axis they have in common. A symmetry-free exact-$\chi$ subset dynamic program, with no canonicalisation anywhere, was run on 2,191 real candidates drawn from both new cells and agreed on every one.
Third implementation. A Python reimplementation written against the report's prose rather than against the scanner (set-partition chromatic number, itertools cliques) agrees exactly on seven classes, including the order-13 class $(8,13)$.
The filters were tested for vacuity. At $(7,13)$ the $K_k$-free filter was switched off and the cell re-run in full: still 0 survivors, so at $k = 7$ the filter is demonstrably inert and not merely justified. At $(7,12)$, $(6,11)$ and $(5,11)$ both filters were removed (up to 495 million graphs), again with 0 survivors. $(5,11)$ is the informative one: $k = 5$ is outside Proposition 9's $k \ge 6$ range, so both filters had to come off, and the answer there is fixed independently by the proved $k \le 5$ theorem. The filter-free scan returns what the theorem requires.
A check a reader can run, needing nothing of ours beyond nauty:
geng -q -c -d8 13 | wc -l # 77,423,446 the whole (7,13) space
geng -q -c -d7 13 0/1000 | wc -l # 10,607,826 one shard of (6,13)
Two ways to get a plausible wrong number instead of an error. The degree flag is $k+1$, not $k$: Proposition 9 gives $\delta \ge k+1$, so $k = 6$ is -d7 and $k = 7$ is -d8, and using -dk returns a larger, correct-looking count of the wrong universe. And geng's res/mod is 0-based, so 0/1000 is the first shard; 1/1000 is the second and gives 9,044,744. The report states that its own 1/1000 shard of $(6,13)$ "produced 10,607,826 graphs", which is our res=0, not our res=1. Almost certainly 1-based prose for the first shard, but the report's output files are gone (see below), so it cannot be settled.
Trust boundary. geng is the enumeration oracle. "Every graph on 13 vertices up to isomorphism" rests on the standard correctness of nauty 2.8.8 and 2.9.3, built from source on each host; the canonical distribution host served an expired TLS certificate, so the tarball came from the ANU mirror, and the binaries are validated behaviourally (the known count of 853 connected graphs on 7 vertices, and identical stream hashes across four builds) rather than by an authenticated checksum. The candidate space itself rests on a cited theorem and not on this computation: Proposition 9 for $\delta \ge k+1$, on which the completeness of the census is conditional. The $K_k$-free restriction is not a second condition — the elementary clique argument above justifies it, and at $(7,13)$ the filter was switched off and the cell re-run regardless. Lemma 2 belongs to the Tihany framing, where it converts a finite counterexample into an induced double-critical subgraph; the census claim does not use it. The two production passes share one scanner source file, so a shared algorithmic bug would survive both; the paired algorithms, the symmetry-free oracle and the Python reimplementation cover that axis, but the reimplementation only reached order-13 $k = 8$. None of this is Lean-verified, and the problem page's linked formal statement (google-deepmind/formal-conjectures) is statement-only with every proof sorry; nothing here changes that. The report's own code and output links are dead — four 404s — so its three published SHA-256 values are uncheckable and everything above was reimplemented from its prose.
What order 13 does not settle. This is finite evidence about graphs on 13 vertices and nothing more. It says nothing about Erdős–Lovász Tihany beyond that finite statement: not about the other unsettled $(a,b)$ pairs, and not about the $a = 2$ branch in general. The missing lemma — no noncomplete connected double-critical $k$-chromatic graph for $k \ge 6$, at any order — is exactly where it was, and a census cannot supply it. There is no asymptotic content here and no growth claim from the table; the counts are what they are at $n = 13$. Order 14 was not attempted: $(6,14)$ scales by roughly the factor $12 \to 13$ did, which is on the order of $10^4$ core-hours. This is not a proof claim, and it is not submitted as one.
The scanner, the third implementation, the planted controls, the run and harvest scripts and every per-shard log from all four passes — the totals re-derive from the logs alone — are at github.com/bitterlemma/erdos-628 (MIT; the README states the exact build and check commands).
This contribution is from the Bitter Lemma project ([email protected] — monitored; artifact requests answered). The computation, the logs and this text were produced with Claude (Anthropic) under human direction and review; both new cells were re-verified by independent passes that did not produce the claim.

 This problem is usually referred to as the Erdős-Lovász Tihany Conjecture. For an up-to-date overview, see Song's survey "The Erdős-Lovász Tihany Conjecture -- a survey'' (PDF). The survey records many additional positive cases beyond the ones already listed on this page. For example, this conjecture holds for every graph \(G\) with independence number \(\alpha(G)\ge 3\) that has no hole of length \(\ell\) with \(4\le \ell \le 2\alpha(G)-1\); see (arXiv:1805.11437) for this result.
A recent progress not covered in the survey is due to Longbrake and Tariq (arXiv:2406.15164).
